passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within the common law of contracts, for it operates as an equitable corrective to the rigors of the consideration requirement rather than as an independent principle of contractual obligation. Under classical contract doctrine, a promise is legally enforceable only when the promisee provides consideration — that is, something of legal value bargained for and given in exchange for the promise. Yet this rule, however coherent in theory, produces harsh results when a promisor makes a clear, unambiguous promise, the promisee reasonably relies upon it to their detriment, and the promisor subsequently seeks to withdraw. It was largely in response to such situations that Anglo-American courts began, in the latter half of the nineteenth century, to develop what would eventually be codified in Section 90 of the American Restatement (Second) of Contracts: the principle that a promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce reliance, and that does induce such reliance, is enforceable to the extent necessary to avoid injustice.

The difficulty, however, lies not in articulating the doctrine but in applying it consistently. Two elements of Section 90's formulation have generated persistent disagreement among courts. The first is the requirement that reliance be "reasonable" — a criterion that courts have interpreted both narrowly, demanding objective evidence that any person in the promisee's position would have acted similarly, and broadly, asking only whether this particular promisee's reliance was not irrational given the circumstances. The second, and more contentious, element is the phrase "to the extent necessary to avoid injustice," which courts have taken to license two distinct and often incompatible remedial approaches: some courts award expectation damages, placing the promisee in the position they would have occupied had the promise been performed; others award only reliance damages, compensating merely for out-of-pocket losses incurred in reliance on the promise. The choice between these measures is not merely technical — expectation damages can be vastly larger — and the absence of a uniform rule has left plaintiffs uncertain of what remedy to seek and courts uncertain of what to award.

This doctrinal inconsistency is particularly regrettable because it undermines the equitable rationale that prompted the doctrine's development in the first place. A promisee who reasonably reorganizes her affairs upon a firm assurance and then receives only partial compensation has not been made whole; the injustice the doctrine was designed to remedy persists. Some commentators have argued that courts should abandon the remedial ambiguity entirely and adopt a uniform expectation-damages rule whenever reliance is established, on the ground that anything less fails to honor the promisee's legitimate expectations. Others maintain that reliance damages are the more principled measure because promissory estoppel is, after all, a substitute for a true contract, and to award expectation damages would be to grant the promisee more than the equitable circumstances warrant. Whether the courts will resolve this tension through legislative intervention or through the gradual consolidation of case law remains to be seen; one hopes, however, that the resolution will be guided by a clear commitment to the doctrine's foundational purpose of preventing detrimental reliance from going uncompensated.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel was developed as an equitable response to the harsh results of the consideration requirement, and courts should uniformly award expectation damages when it applies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel arose to address injustices produced by the consideration requirement, inconsistent judicial interpretation of two key elements of the doctrine has prevented it from reliably achieving its remedial purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Section 90 of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts represents the most satisfactory codification of promissory estoppel, but courts have applied its remedial provisions incorrectly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinction between expectation damages and reliance damages is the central unresolved question in American contract law, and legislative intervention is the only viable solution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel has replaced classical contract doctrine in Anglo-American courts because the consideration requirement has proven unworkable in most commercial disputes.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the doctrine's equitable origins (paragraph 1), identifies two specific sources of interpretive inconsistency (paragraph 2), and argues that this inconsistency undermines the doctrine's purpose (paragraph 3). B integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: Too narrow — the passage does not endorse the expectation-damages rule; it presents it as one contested position among two.
explanations.C: The passage does not claim the Restatement is the most satisfactory codification, nor does it say courts apply it 'incorrectly' — rather, courts interpret it inconsistently.
explanations.D: Too strong and too broad — this describes one element of the problem but excludes the 'reasonableness of reliance' element and misstates the author's view of legislative intervention (presented as one possibility, not the only solution).
explanations.E: The passage does not claim promissory estoppel has replaced classical doctrine; it is described as a corrective supplement, and the consideration requirement is not called unworkable.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under classical contract doctrine a promise is legally enforceable only when

choices.label: A
choices.text: the promisee has relied on the promise to their detriment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the promisor had a reasonable expectation that the promisee would rely on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the promisee provides something of legal value bargained for and given in exchange for the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a court determines that enforcing the promise is necessary to avoid injustice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the promise is clear and unambiguous and is made by a party with the capacity to contract.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: 'a promise is legally enforceable only when the promisee provides consideration — that is, something of legal value bargained for and given in exchange for the promise.' C is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: This describes a condition for promissory estoppel, not classical doctrine.
explanations.B: This describes an element of Section 90's formulation, not the classical consideration requirement.
explanations.D: This paraphrases the 'to the extent necessary to avoid injustice' standard from Section 90, not classical doctrine.
explanations.E: Capacity is not mentioned in the passage; the passage focuses on consideration as the enforcement requirement.

questions.questionStem: The passage identifies which of the following as the two elements of Section 90's formulation that have generated the most persistent disagreement among courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The requirement that the promise be unambiguous and the requirement that the promisor have bargained for reliance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reasonableness of the promisee's reliance and the phrase 'to the extent necessary to avoid injustice.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: The definition of consideration and the appropriate measure of damages in contract disputes generally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The requirement that reliance be detrimental and the requirement that the promisor intend to induce that reliance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The distinction between equitable and legal remedies and the appropriate jurisdiction for promissory estoppel claims.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly identifies 'the requirement that reliance be reasonable' and 'the phrase to the extent necessary to avoid injustice' as the two elements generating persistent disagreement.
explanations.A: Neither 'unambiguous promise' nor 'bargained-for reliance' is identified as a contested element of Section 90 — these relate to classical doctrine.
explanations.C: The passage is not about the definition of consideration in general; that belongs to classical doctrine, not Section 90.
explanations.D: Detrimental reliance and intent to induce are touched on but not identified as the two contested elements generating persistent judicial disagreement.
explanations.E: Jurisdictional questions and the equitable/legal remedy distinction as such are not the two contested elements the passage names.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts that award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases are acting contrary to the equitable rationale that gave rise to the doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A promisee who incurs substantial out-of-pocket losses in reasonable reliance on a promise has suffered an injustice if those losses are not fully compensated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be abolished and replaced with a statutory scheme that precisely defines when promises are enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be eliminated from classical contract doctrine because it produces uniformly unjust outcomes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts that award only reliance damages in promissory estoppel cases are always acting consistently with the doctrine's foundational purpose.

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'a promisee who reasonably reorganizes her affairs upon a firm assurance and then receives only partial compensation has not been made whole; the injustice the doctrine was designed to remedy persists.' This directly supports B.
explanations.A: The passage does not condemn expectation damages as contrary to the equitable rationale — it presents expectation damages as one of two contested approaches, and the commentators who favor it are not dismissed.
explanations.C: The author expresses hope that the doctrine's foundational purpose will guide resolution; abolishing the doctrine entirely is not suggested.
explanations.D: The author describes the consideration requirement as producing 'harsh results' in some situations, not uniformly unjust outcomes; this overreaches the passage.
explanations.E: The passage presents reliance damages as one contested view; the author does not endorse it as 'always' consistent with the doctrine's purpose.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident that legislative reform will soon resolve the competing remedial approaches adopted by different courts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: skeptical that promissory estoppel can ever be applied consistently given the inherently vague language of equitable doctrine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical of the doctrinal inconsistency that has emerged and hopeful that courts will orient any resolution around the doctrine's foundational purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral as between the expectation-damages and reliance-damages approaches, viewing each as an equally valid expression of the doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: dismissive of the commentators who advocate for a uniform expectation-damages rule, on the ground that such a rule exceeds the equitable scope of the doctrine.

explanations.correct: The author calls the inconsistency 'particularly regrettable' and closes with 'one hopes... that the resolution will be guided by a clear commitment to the doctrine's foundational purpose.' This combines criticism of the current state with a qualified hope for principled resolution — precisely what C captures.
explanations.A: The author says legislative intervention is one possibility, not that it will 'soon' occur; 'confident' overstates the author's tone.
explanations.B: The author does not suggest the doctrine is inherently incapable of consistent application; the problem is identified as judicial inconsistency, not structural vagueness beyond remedy.
explanations.D: The author is not neutral — the passage's closing sentence and the description of the inconsistency as 'regrettable' signal clear evaluative investment.
explanations.E: The author presents commentators favoring expectation damages as a coherent position; 'dismissive' mischaracterizes the author's even-handed treatment of both camps.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of expectation damages and reliance damages in the second paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how the phrase 'to the extent necessary to avoid injustice' has produced inconsistent remedial outcomes, thereby supporting the broader claim that the doctrine is applied inconsistently.

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that expectation damages are the more equitable remedy and should be uniformly adopted by courts applying promissory estoppel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain how the consideration requirement in classical contract doctrine was gradually replaced by reliance-based principles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the Restatement (Second) of Contracts deliberately left the remedial question open to allow courts flexibility in achieving equitable outcomes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a historical account of how promissory estoppel was codified in Section 90, tracing its development from nineteenth-century equity courts.

explanations.correct: The second paragraph identifies two contested elements of Section 90; the discussion of expectation vs. reliance damages exemplifies how the second contested element — the 'injustice' phrase — produces divergent outcomes. This supports the paragraph's overarching claim about doctrinal inconsistency, which in turn supports the passage's main argument.
explanations.B: The author presents both approaches even-handedly; the discussion does not argue for expectation damages.
explanations.C: The passage describes promissory estoppel as a corrective supplement to, not a replacement for, classical doctrine.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim the Restatement deliberately left the question open; the ambiguity is treated as a problem, not a designed feature.
explanations.E: The historical account of Section 90's development appears in paragraph 1, not paragraph 2; paragraph 2 is about interpretive disagreement, not codification history.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins are described; two specific interpretive problems with the doctrine are identified and illustrated; the author argues that these problems undermine the doctrine's purpose and expresses hope for a principled resolution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced; a single authoritative interpretation of the doctrine is endorsed; counterarguments to that interpretation are surveyed and dismissed; the author concludes that legislative intervention is required.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing contract-law doctrines are introduced and compared; their respective historical origins are traced; the author argues that one doctrine is superior to the other and should replace it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal problem is identified; a court case illustrating the problem is analyzed in detail; the author uses the case to derive a general principle applicable to all future promissory estoppel claims.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine and the traditional requirement it supplements are described; the doctrine's codification is praised as satisfactory; a single disputed element is analyzed and a resolution is proposed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel, its equitable rationale, and Section 90. Paragraph 2 identifies two contested elements and illustrates their inconsistent judicial application. Paragraph 3 evaluates this inconsistency as undermining the doctrine's purpose and closes with a hope for principled resolution. A follows this sequence accurately.
explanations.B: The passage does not endorse a single interpretation, nor does it dismiss counterarguments; legislative intervention is one possibility, not the author's conclusion.
explanations.C: Only one doctrine (promissory estoppel) is at the center of the passage; classical doctrine is context, not an equal subject. The passage does not argue for replacement.
explanations.D: No specific court case is analyzed in detail; the passage is doctrinal and analytical rather than case-focused.
explanations.E: The Restatement codification is not praised as satisfactory — it is described as generating disagreement. The passage identifies two disputed elements, not one, and does not propose a specific resolution.
